level_problem: Past perfect for an unfulfilled plan is B1-B2; 'have'/'was' are rejected at once by a B1 learner. Acceptable only as review.

answer: we were hoping you might help us with the move
other_correct: were we hoping you might help us with the move
sense_problem: Question order 'were we hoping you might help us with the move?' is grammatical (odd sense, but punctuation is hidden). 'you might help us with the move, we were hoping' is a spoken afterthought order, marginal.

level_problem: 'always' + past continuous for an annoying habit is B2; 'is/has' clash with 'When we were teenagers' and are spotted at once.

answer: we were walking to work every day during the strike
other_correct: during the strike we were walking to work every day
during the strike, every day we were walking to work
every day during the strike we were walking to work
we were walking to work during the strike every day
every day we were walking to work during the strike
sense_problem: Several fronted/end positions of 'every day' and 'during the strike' are correct; 'during the strike we were walking...' is fully natural and must be accepted. Past continuous for a temporary repeated situation is fine, though 'we walked' is the more usual choice.

level_problem: Too easy for C1: a B1 learner solves it at once (basic tense form, distractors are obvious form errors).
Too easy for C1: a B1 learner solves it at once (basic tense form, distractors are obvious form errors). Interrupted past continuous is A2-B1.

answer: I was going to call you but I fell asleep
other_correct: I fell asleep but I was going to call you
level_problem: 'was going to' for an unfulfilled intention is B1-B2.
sense_problem: Swapped clauses 'I fell asleep, but I was going to call you' are grammatical and plausible as an apology (less natural).

answer: this is the third time the lift has broken down this month
other_correct: this is the third time this month the lift has broken down
this month is the third time the lift has broken down
sense_problem: 'this is the third time this month the lift has broken down' is fully natural and must be accepted. 'this month is the third time...' is marginal/wrong. Two 'this' and two 'the' cards make many permutations; check them in the grader.
Fine: 'will have lived' would need only three gaps, so four gaps force the continuous.

level_problem: Present perfect after 'once' for a completed future condition: B2; acceptable.

answer: I've been trying to reach you all afternoon
other_correct: all afternoon I've been trying to reach you
I've been trying all afternoon to reach you
level_problem: Too easy for C1: a B1 learner solves it at once (basic tense form, distractors are obvious form errors). Present perfect continuous with 'all afternoon' is B1.
sense_problem: 'I've been trying all afternoon to reach you' is natural and must be accepted, as must the fronted 'all afternoon'.

level_problem: Too easy for C1: a B1 learner solves it at once (basic tense form, distractors are obvious form errors). 'It's only Tuesday ... this week' + present perfect is A2-B1.

answer: the house is thought to have been built in the 1890s
other_correct: in the 1890s the house is thought to have been built
sense_problem: Fronted 'in the 1890s' is grammatical but unnatural (rule: fronted phrases of this kind are not accepted); the main order is unique.
Good: 'If you have' needs one gap only, so two gaps force 'should have'.

answer: when she was a child she would spend hours in the garden
other_correct: she would spend hours in the garden when she was a child
sense_problem: Both clause orders are correct and must be accepted. 'she would spend hours when she was a child in the garden' is awkward, not acceptable.
Good C1 point (insistent 'will' in an if-clause, Swan). Note: a learner may want plain 'go', but two gaps force 'will go'. 'would go' is wrong for a present habit.

answer: the car wouldn't start this morning so I took the bus
other_correct: this morning the car wouldn't start so I took the bus
the car wouldn't start so I took the bus this morning
the car wouldn't start so this morning I took the bus
sense_problem: Several positions of 'this morning' are correct; at least the fronted one and the end-of-sentence one must be accepted.

wrong_options_that_fit: 'will be' after 'in case' is a typical learner error but is heard in speech; not standard, so OK as distractor.
sense_problem: 'in case ... should be' is correct but formal; the natural form ('are') is not on the cards, so the model sentence sounds a little stilted after an informal imperative.

answer: you should have told me you were going to be late
other_correct: should you have told me you were going to be late
you were going to be late, you should have told me
sense_problem: Question order is grammatical but odd in sense; 'you were going to be late, you should have told me' is a spoken (comma-spliced) order, marginal.

answer: he can't have been at home last night
other_correct: last night he can't have been at home
sense_problem: Fronted 'last night' is grammatical (less natural); accept it.

level_problem: 'can' for typical possibility is B1; 'are being dangerous' is not a believable C1 mistake.
Too easy for C1: a B1 learner solves it at once (basic tense form, distractors are obvious form errors).
sense_problem: Distractors 'could'/'are' are not believable here: 'could allowed' is not a form; 'are allowed' clashes with 'was closed'.

answer: she may be clever but she has no common sense
other_correct: she has no common sense but she may be clever
clever she may be but she has no common sense
sense_problem: 'Clever she may be, but she has no common sense' (fronted adjective, concessive) is correct literary C1 English. Swapped clauses are grammatical but lose the concessive sense (less natural).

level_problem: Too easy for C1: a B1 learner solves it at once (basic tense form, distractors are obvious form errors). 'could see' is A2-B1.
sense_problem: 'managed' is not a believable distractor ('managed see' is not a form; 'managed to see' would need 'to').

answer: they might have been delayed by the snow
other_correct: might they have been delayed by the snow
sense_problem: Question order 'might they have been delayed by the snow?' is grammatical (hidden punctuation).

other_correct: drink
no
drinks
no
wrong_options_that_fit: 'drink no coffee' (subjunctive + 'no') is correct, if less natural. 'drinks no coffee' after 'recommended that' is accepted in informal British English by Swan (ordinary present after verbs of recommending), though tense backshift would suggest 'drank'.
sense_problem: Serious: two-card answers 'drink no' and arguably 'drinks no' are correct. The 'no' card breaks the uniqueness; replace it with a clear non-form.

answer: I'd rather you had asked me before taking my car
other_correct: before taking my car I'd rather you had asked me
sense_problem: Fronted 'before taking my car' is grammatical but awkward; main order unique.
Mandative subjunctive is correct; British English would more often say 'should not be', but the model is fine. 'be not' is archaic, so correctly rejected.

answer: the committee insisted that the decision be made public
other_correct: the public committee insisted that the decision be made
the committee insisted that the public decision be made
sense_problem: Odd but grammatical alternatives exist because 'public' can be an attributive adjective and 'make a decision' needs no complement ('insisted that the decision be made'). Less natural; consider whether the grader needs them.

level_problem: Fixed idiom: a learner either knows it or not; fine for C1 but not a grammar decision.

answer: the landlord requested that all tenants should leave their keys at reception
other_correct: the landlord requested that tenants should leave all their keys at reception
sense_problem: 'requested that tenants should leave all their keys at reception' is correct (different but sensible meaning) and must be accepted. Also 'at reception' with no article is right; good.
'The news is getting better than we expected' is slightly odd ('is better than we expected' is the usual phrase), but grammatical.

answer: the majority of the residents are against the new car park
other_correct: the majority of the new residents are against the car park
sense_problem: Serious: 'the majority of the new residents are against the car park' is fully correct and sensible; three 'the' cards and 'new' can go in two places.

other_correct: still
makes
wrong_options_that_fit: 'still makes' (singular after 'one of the ... who') is very common in speech and accepted informally by Swan, though plural is the standard.
sense_problem: Good C1 point; but the grader should decide whether informal 'makes' is accepted.

wrong_options_that_fit: 'has been' ('There's been three cars...') is common in informal speech but non-standard in writing.

answer: two thirds of the money has already been spent
other_correct: two thirds of the money has been spent already
two thirds of the money has been already spent
sense_problem: 'has been spent already' is natural and must be accepted; 'has been already spent' is less natural but occurs.

answer: neither the teacher nor the students were happy with the results
other_correct: neither the students nor the teacher were happy with the results
sense_problem: Swapped order with 'were' is common and accepted in informal style (Swan: plural verb with neither...nor is usual informally), though proximity would require 'was'. Decide whether to accept.

level_problem: 'in which' is B2; 'where' cannot fill two gaps, so the task is forced; acceptable.

answer: this is the problem we need to deal with
other_correct: the problem we need to deal with is this
is this the problem we need to deal with
sense_problem: Serious: 'the problem we need to deal with is this' (statement) and 'is this the problem we need to deal with?' (question) are both correct.

other_correct: of
them
wrong_options_that_fit: 'both of them live abroad' is a comma splice in writing but very common in speech.

answer: the matter is being looked into by the police
other_correct: is the matter being looked into by the police
sense_problem: Question order 'is the matter being looked into by the police?' is grammatical (hidden punctuation).

answer: she's not an easy person to work with
sense_problem: Fine.
Fine: 'Reading' alone fills one gap only.

answer: not wanting to wake the children we spoke in whispers
other_correct: we spoke in whispers not wanting to wake the children
wanting not to wake the children we spoke in whispers
sense_problem: Both clause orders are correct and must be accepted; 'wanting not to wake' is correct but less natural.
Absolute construction is correct but stilted with a plain adjective; 'The weather being so bad' would be more natural. 'was bad' gives a comma splice (correctly wrong).
Capital letters on cards reveal which cards can start the sentence (only 'On'/'If'), narrowing choice.

answer: the woman sitting next to me on the plane was a famous actress
other_correct: the woman sitting on the plane next to me was a famous actress
on the plane the woman sitting next to me was a famous actress
the famous actress sitting next to me on the plane was a woman
sense_problem: 'sitting on the plane next to me' is correct (less natural); fronted 'on the plane' is fine; 'the famous actress ... was a woman' is grammatical but absurd.

answer: generally speaking people here are very friendly
other_correct: people here are generally speaking very friendly
people here generally speaking are very friendly
people here are very friendly generally speaking
speaking generally people here are very friendly
sense_problem: Serious: the disjunct 'generally speaking' can go first, mid or last; all must be accepted or the sentence changed.

answer: no sooner had the film started than the power went off
other_correct: the film had no sooner started than the power went off
sense_problem: Serious: the non-inverted 'the film had no sooner started than the power went off' is standard correct English (Swan, Hewings) and uses all cards.

answer: at the top of the hill stands an old church
other_correct: an old church stands at the top of the hill
sense_problem: Serious: the uninverted 'an old church stands at the top of the hill' is correct and more usual; the task cannot force the inversion.

answer: all we need now is a bit of luck
other_correct: now all we need is a bit of luck
all we need is a bit of luck now
a bit of luck is all we need now
now a bit of luck is all we need
sense_problem: Serious: 'now all we need is a bit of luck' and 'a bit of luck is all we need now' are fully natural.

level_problem: 'be being' + adjective for behaviour is B2; fine as review.

other_correct: we're hoping you can join us on Saturday for dinner
on Saturday we're hoping you can join us for dinner
level_problem: Too easy for C1: a B1 learner orders it without difficulty.
sense_problem: 'join us on Saturday for dinner' is fully natural and must be accepted.
Present simple 'tells me' for news is a nice C1 point; fine.

answer: we're loving every minute of our holiday
level_problem: Too easy for C1: only one possible order, short and everyday (B1).
